utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Marcussen, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. The next witness is Halit Berisha, but I understand that one of my colleagues on the other side has an objection that you might want to deal with before we bring in the witness. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I was alerted to that. That is just to confirm that the witness is available and that's what your intention is. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has an objection to the relevance of party's statements --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, they cannot hear Mr. Zecevic. Other microphones are on in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Should I start from the very beginning again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The Defence has an objection -- the Defence has an objection -- [Interpretation] -- as to the relevance of parts of the statement and transcript of witness Halit Berisha. Therefore, the Defence takes the following position in view of stipulating agreed facts and relevant regulations -- rather, laws that were in force at the time of the indictment. And this is presented in our motion to the Trial Chamber dated the 31st of August -- or rather, the 1st of September, 2006. As a matter of fact, Witness Berisha in part of his statement and also in part of the transcript from the Milosevic trial speaks of events that occurred in the period from 1989 up until 1991. These facts, in the view of the Defence, do not prove -- or rather, do not challenge a single one of the counts of this indictment. These facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean the objection here is to paragraph 2 of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me consult with the statement, Your Honour. Exactly, paragraph 2 and paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, paragraph 3 is of little moment I suspect, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, well, paragraph 2 in essence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's -- I mean, his previous history of working, where he worked, and being unemployed is of some marginal background relevance. But paragraph 2, I notice, is your -- the one to which you're opposed. Now, you say that this is because of having stipulated to certain facts and legislation. Is that right? Or have I -- it's -- what you said in the beginning isn't really terribly clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what it's about, Your Honour -- or rather, we are challenging the relevance of parts of the statement in view of the fact that they pertain to the period from 1989 until 1991. This position is one that we already presented in our motion to the Trial Chamber dated the 31st of August that had to do with the order issued by the Trial Chamber regarding stipulations. To that effect, I tried to show the consistency of our position, the position of the Defence, to the Trial Chamber from the point of view of this particular aspect. [In English] May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These facts that are mentioned in the statement and in part of the transcript of Mr. Halit Berisha were relevant for the Milosevic case in view of the nature of this case, the position -- the office held by Slobodan Milosevic and the fact that the indictment against Mr. Milosevic pertained to the period of conflicts in the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia as well -- or rather, Croatia and Bosnia as well, too. In this case, however, the period relevant to the indictment pertains to alleged crimes committed after the 23rd of March, 1999, and at the time when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in existence. The SFRY ceased to exist on the 27th of April, 1992, when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established and when a new constitution was passed for the new state union of Serbia and Montenegro. This change of the constitution also meant a change in the entire social political system of the state. It meant that socialism disappeared and also social itself management as the basis of the social and economic system of the country, as well as other foundations upon which the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was based. The constitution of the FRY on the other hand is based on a completely social-political system. First and foremost, the rule of law, the rights of citizens, market economy, democracy, and political pluralism. After the constitution was adopted. After the constitution of The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted in accordance with the time limits in the constitutional law for the implementation of the constitution, a certain number of regulations of the former SFRY was no longer in force, whereas other regulations were changed and amended within a certain time period and brought into accord with the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The provisions of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the paragraph on constitutionality and legality, notably article 1 to 15 envisages that the constitutions of the member states, that is to say Serbia and Montenegro, as well as their regulations have to be brought into accordance with the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This basically means that the regulations of the member republics after the constitution of the FRY was adopted had to be changed, too, because they had to be brought into accord with the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. For these reasons, we believe that as far as this case is concerned, events and incidents and acts that were committed in a state that ceased to exist are of no relevance for this case. We believe that our position contributes to focussing this court proceeding on relevant facts from the indictment. Presenting evidence that goes beyond that scope would necessarily bring about a serious extension of the court proceedings. Since the Defence will have no other alternative but to adduce evidence that will show that the history of Kosovo-Metohija and the development of the autonomy of that province did not start in 1989 but considerably before that. Perhaps in 1946 or we can even go back to the end of the 19th century and the Prizren League. In our view, this kind of situation would necessarily lead to this trial being one where we would deal with history and hearing numerous experts, who would present facts related to history and the genesis of the autonomy of Kosovo-Metohija. Our position is that that is not the objective of this trial, and therefore we suggest to the Trial Chamber not to allow anyone to call evidence that is not relevant to this indictment, because on the one hand it would lead to a waste of precious time and on the other hand if the Trial Chamber would consider these facts to be relevant, the Defence would be compelled to respond in an appropriate manner to facts presented in this way. [In English] Thank you, Your Honours, this was my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just ask you a couple of questions for clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In both 1990 and 1999, the boundaries of the Republic of Serbia were identical. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The boundaries of the Republic of Serbia were correct, not the boundaries of Republika Srpska. Maybe it was a misinterpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The boundaries of the Republic of Serbia were the same in 1990 as in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the boundaries of Kosovo within the Republic of Serbia were the same in 1990 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And just one other thing. What does the indictment say about the involvement of your client and Mr. Sainovic in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our view, in our view, Your Honour, the indictment deals with facts from 1981 to 1996 or 1997 only in paragraphs 82 through 94 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- As part of the context for the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, there's a reference in paragraph 89 to Milosevic implementing policy through others, including the first and second accused here. But there's no indication I think in the indictment that they held particular posts in 1990, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a separate objection, whether you want to hear that now or deal with the one Mr. Zecevic made first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. On you go, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on and state your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, last night I think the e-mail was sent around 8.00 p.m. I didn't receive it until after 9.00, and I'm sure that most of my colleagues didn't receive it that early. The Prosecution notified us that they had prepared a number of excerpts from the transcript of the testimony of this witness in the Milosevic case and that there were some changes made in it by the witness and that they intended to use it today as an exhibit. That doesn't come even close to complying with the notice requirements of -- of your order on procedure entered at the beginning of this case. And on that basis alone, I object to that. If there is some reasonable that objection would be overruled, then I have a specific objection to various parts of that transcript being admitted in this case, but I'll stand right now on my objection as to the entire transcript coming in. In addition, we -- we did receive notice that the Prosecution would seek to admit Exhibits P777 through P794 through this witness, and these consist of -- of a bunch of documents and stuff that this witness says he found lying around or were on a CD -- or not a CD, a disk that was handed to him upon his return to Suhareke. There is absolutely no indication that these exhibits are what they appear to be. They have not been authenticated in any way, and in fact there is indication that they are not authentic. And that can be found with regard to Exhibit 782, which this witness said in his testimony Milosevic was -- was handwritten by a Serb, that he was certain that it was written by a Serb. Your Honour will notice that the -- if you look that the translation into English of that handwritten notation in 782, the translator makes a note saying that the writer seems unfamiliar with the Cyrillic alphabet, indicating that it was probably written by somebody who was unfamiliar with writing in Cyrillic, which probably wouldn't fit in with what it's purported to be. In any event, I think all those attachments are irrelevant to the issues we're dealing with here and they have no authenticity to them. They're -- they haven't been identified by anyone as being authentic, and I think they should all be ruled out of evidence and denied, the admission denied. I want to speak very specifically about 781 and 782. 781 and 782 seem to be an effort to -- to kind of sneak in through the backdoor what you ruled out on Monday in terms of the village of Trnje, because that's apparently what the contention is, that these documents speak about is the events in the village of Trnje that were ruled inadmissible with the Witness K-82 on Monday. So that would be I think the essence of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. The document on the screen is P78 -- is it 782? But what we have there is a typewritten version. Is there an original document? Ah, you -- well, on your screen I think we see the original. Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'll address the points raised by both of my learned colleagues, but I'd like to comment first on something Mr. Ackerman said towards the end of his submissions. Well, first of all I should say that actually it was not my intention to -- to seek 781 and 782 admitted today through the witness. I'm not sure the -- we will not be relying on those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which ones are they on the list in the statement, the last page of the statement? I think we've got items 1 to 15 listed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They're number 4, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Number 4. They're both number 4, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's two sides -- a picture and on the back side something is written on the picture. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So it's 4 and 5 then, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood it was 4, but it could be 4 and 5, but I think it's just 4. I think that's just a two-page document basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. So -- anyway, carry on, please, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So to that extent there shouldn't be any issue. To the issue of sneaking exhibits into the record that have been disallowed, I just think I should note that we filed the -- our witness notification last week before Your Honours ruled on K-82, so I find that -- that suggestion a little misplaced. With respect to the relevancy of paragraph 2 of Halit Berisha's statement and also the documents that Mr. Ackerman has objected to, we submit that these documents are clearly relevant to paragraph 88 of the indictment. They are essentially -- the fact that Mr. Berisha was dismissed as a mayor was part of, in our submission, an increasingly discriminatory policy against Albanians and we are not seeking to rely on the legal nature of these documents. We would be putting these documents in to show some of the factual background to the development on the -- of the conflicts in -- in Serbia and in Kosovo. So we submit that these documents are highly relevant to the determination of whether or not there was a plan that evolved over time and led to the events in 1999, culminated in 1999. I don't have much further to really add on that unless Your Honours have specific questions on this. Maybe another thing to clarify is that Mr. Ackerman referred to documents on a CD and documents found in -- found by Halit Berisha in the municipal building in Suva Reka. None of the exhibits that we are seeking to tender through the witness were found -- are those that originate from the CD. P77 through P -- sorry, P777 through P794 are all documents that he himself found in the municipal building and he would be able to explain today to the Court how he found them, the process by which he gathered them, and how he provided them to the Office of the Prosecutor. So we submit that the witness should be allowed to testify about -- this evidence about his dismissal as a mayor should be admitted and we should put these documents to him and at least wait for the determination on their admissibility until we have heard from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it you say that proving paragraph 88 of the indictment will contribute to the determination of the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm not entirely sure that -- it seems that we're getting into the scope of the indictment, which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're anxious to understand it, you see, because we obviously were at cross-purposes going by the debate we had on Monday. And we have taken a decision which is obviously contrary to the view that the Prosecution had of the scope of the indictment. So I think it's legitimate of the Bench to seek from time to time clarification of what's intended to be shown by proving particular points, and I'd like to know if you can help me - and if you can't, please say so - what you think will be achieved that will assist us by proving what's set out in paragraph 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In our pre-trial brief we have explained -- we set out the background for the joint criminal enterprise that we say came into existence -- that was in existence at the time of the crime -- specific incidents charged in the indictment. In order to -- for Your Honours to make a determination of whether or not there was a joint criminal enterprise in 1999, we submit that it is relevant to look at the historical context to some extent, and paragraph 88 of the indictment is part of that historical context. It's the Prosecution's submission that the issue of the autonomy of Kosovo was a crucial political issue -- was a crucial political issue for many Serbs. It was important for Milosevic to come to power and hold on to power. We have set out how there was initial attempts to achieve alteration of the ethnic balance in Kosovo through various practical and legislative means. We have explained how that eventually seems to have been considered not to have been efficient enough, and eventually we ended up with the mass deportation and expulsion that occurred in 1999. So that is the relevancy of this evidence. We submit that it's highly important for the Trial Chamber to hear this evidence and to have it on record and to be able to consider that when you finally deliberate on the issues of whether or not there was a joint criminal enterprise and also the intent of the accused in these sort of bigger issues in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you. That is helpful to hear these points that you have expressed. But what you have not dealt with so far is the late notification of changes to the transcript and the objection that's taken to the transcript in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Sorry, I forgot that. Yes, it is correct. Halit Berisha only arrived here in the evening the day before yesterday. We were only able to meet with him yesterday. He has made -- when we met with him and put certain excerpts of his testimony in the Milosevic case to him, with a view to see if we could have that part of his evidence admitted under Rule 89(F), the transcript was read back to him and he had certain, in my view -- in my submission, cosmetic changes to what was in the transcript and a few clarifications. Some of the clarifications, if I could -- I don't know if you would like me to go through them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, one of them I know is the difference between life and death, but the others may be cosmetic. That may be the only one that's significant. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I think the one about life and death really -- I'm just looking for it so we can go into more detail. Yes, it's at -- in the Milosevic transcript it's page 7.462. I don't think this -- well, I don't know if it is the Defence position that there is an issue about whether or not Jashar Berisha got killed on the 26th of March, 1999. I would think that that is not the case. So really -- and if one looks at paragraph -- at line 6 of the page that I've just referred to, it's quite clear that what's being talked about here is that events on the 28th of March. That's clearly two days after the brother had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: "My brother was still at the gas station." Well, it could even have been true in the witness's mind in that he could still be lying dead there as far as he was concerned, but what he clarified with me was just that the brother had been killed at the gas station. I'm -- in my submission, this is not a material change to the evidence of this witness. It really is a minor clarification of something that has gone into the transcript. And the other ones are really rather small. One of them is a consequence of something that was corrected with respect to how Halit Berisha and one of his brothers separated at one point and the brother tried to get to Albania. Now, that is wrong. It's wrongly set out in the -- in Halit Berisha's statement, and a correction was made in the Milosevic transcript. And it looks like there was some confusion later on in the transcript. And those -- little things like that have been changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think you've addressed that sufficiently. Thank you, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think maybe you are -- the Chamber is viewing this without having -- me having given you all the information I need to have given you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I do want you also to separately address the subsidiary objection you have to parts of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I will. Unless I missed something, we were given a 65 ter list of exhibits for this witness and it had a list of exhibits to be used with this witness. The statement was not contained in that list, the transcript from the Milosevic case was not contained in that list. What was contained in that list are all those attachments we've been talking about today, P777 through P794, a couple of photographs and a couple of maps, and that's it. So this isn't a cosmetic change to something we've been notified was going to be used as an exhibit with this witness; it's a completely new exhibit. They had not notified us they were going to use the Milosevic transcript as an exhibit; second, they had not even notified us they were going to use the witness's statement as an 89(F) statement. And I understand they intend to do that today also and I'm not objecting to that, even though there's been no notification. Now, if I missed something that came to us by e-mail or something like that, maybe I will find out that I'm speaking out of turn here, but I don't think so. I don't think any of us had any notice regarding this. Now, if you want me to go into the specific parts of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just before you do, I'm trying to be realistic about this situation and where you've been given a statement which in this case is a statement dated the 17th of August, 2001, and a witness then comes here, I find it difficult to see that there can be any real objection in principle to the witness going into the witness box and being asked by the Prosecution to confirm whether the statement's accurate or not and -- it simply avoids leading viva voce the evidence that otherwise would be presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I already told you, I make no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I then extend that to the transcript. If the transcript was at least on the 65 ter list, and I don't think you've told me it wasn't listed --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you told me it wasn't listed against this witness. Just -- was it not listed at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At all?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at the one with regard to this witness. I don't know why it would be on any other 65 ter list because it is this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's correct, we have not listed the transcript of -- or indeed the statement as an exhibit early on. Halit Berisha was initially indicated to be a live witness, and it would probably have even been inappropriate of us to make his statement an exhibit in such circumstances. We have -- it really is a question of time. In my submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's not a question of time. If you're going to present exhibits that have never been on the list then there's a method of doing that, and that is for you to seek leave, if you haven't sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, our understanding of the -- of the 89(F) procedure is that we would get the witness into court. We would confirm with the witness whether or not the witness statement of the witness reflects his evidence today. If that is the case, then we would ask to have the statement tendered. We did in our witness notification that we filed last week indicate that Halit Berisha was going to be an 89(F) witness. Now, we had not had an opportunity to speak to Halit Berisha until then, so we were not able to indicate that his statement and excerpts from the Milosevic transcript would indeed be the 89(F) material. Had we done so but would have found ourselves in the situation where there would have been substantial changes, we would have had to replace the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know if he has a telephone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: He does have a telephone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why does nobody do these things before witnesses come here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, to my knowledge the witness didn't have a copy of his statement and he certainly didn't have the transcript from the Milosevic case, which is in English and which in any event he couldn't have read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have somebody in Pristina with a fax?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We could probably have faxed things to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. I mean, I continue to be amazed at the difficulties that the Prosecution claim in preparing witnesses. Now, we are told that there are resource problems, but every witness that comes here seems to be speaking to historical statements or old transcripts, to which nothing has been done until they arrive a couple of days before giving evidence. And many of them have given evidence in the Milosevic trial. Now, it's very -- I wonder what has been taking up all your time in dealing with the preparation of these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just to try to address some of the facts. This is a situation where the witness actually has not changed his statement in any substantial way. Now, there have been instances where that have happened, but this is actually, in my submission, a situation where there is not a substantial problem in terms of changing the evidence. Now, also we have moved in witness forward because of the decision on K-52 [sic], the original plan was that this witness would have testified next week and we would have had much more time to clarify these issues. In order to try to accommodate the Court and have witnesses available, we fast-tracked the witness. We proofed him last night and this morning only to be able to put him before the Court today. Yes, there are resource issues, yes there are problems, but I think this is a situation where we have done everything we could in order to provide things as speedily as we could to the Defence and make sure that we have witnesses in the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, Mr. Ackerman, going back to being realistic about -- sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I came down because I heard something Mr. Ackerman said that I thought I needed to address to the Court. Perhaps Mr. Ackerman doesn't remember, but yesterday afternoon I had a conversation with at least one representative for each of the six accused, advising him that this witness had just arrived, he was being proofed by Mr. Marcussen, that we intended to propose him as a 89(F) statement. That he was going to gray that his original ICTY statement was substantially correct. That was going to be his 89(F) statement along with some excerpts from his transcript, as I understood from Mr. Marcussen that he was aware that he was going to do something with that. I pointed out to them -- they understood I had a problem I with the 48-hour rule because we anticipated he was going to be testifying on Thursday and we would have been doing this Tuesday, but now he's testifying on Wednesday. I told them also that if it turned out that he had something substantially new and different, then of course we would understand that they wouldn't -- not be in a position or willing to waive the 48-hour rule because notice wouldn't be adequate for that -- new kinds of things. But I did indicate, and I thought I understood from all of them that if there was not a substantial difference between his original ICTY statement and the transcripts, then -- then they probably wouldn't have a big disagreement about that. Now, I don't know if I misunderstood what Mr. Ackerman said earlier, but that's why I came down, to bring that to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Now, Mr. Ackerman, you want to address individual items of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, first of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You should do it, bearing in mind that one other way of dealing with this, of course, is to have the same evidence led live if it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think it will become clear that it's a problem either way. With regard to what Mr. Hannis just said, it's absolutely correct that he came and talked to us all, talked to me about that problem, and I told him I had no objection with regard to an 89(F) statement. I don't believe he ever mentioned excerpts from a transcript; I was quite surprised to receive them last night. And if he did mention them, my mind was elsewhere when that happened. But I don't think so. Now, the problem with the transcript, Your Honour, begins with the 65 ter notification. The 65 ter summary and the one, two, three, four, fifth paragraph advises us that this witness will testify that a Serb policeman neighbour came to his home and told him that he must go to Albania or paramilitaries would kill him. That is totally consistent with -- with what he says in his statement, and that is on -- in paragraph on page 3 of the statement, which is destined to become an 89(F) statement. The problem we run into is when we get to this transcript that they now want to put into evidence, which goes beyond the 65 ter summary, they want you to consider testimony from the witness at page 7462 where he says regarding this incident: This policeman who came said: "You have to make -- to get yourselves ready within 15 minutes because they might come. The army and the police will come and they're going to kill you all." So that's one place where it deviates dramatically from what we were told with regard to the 65 ter, and they're now trying to bring that in that direction, in that way. The other place is at page 7472. It begins there. The particular part that I'm concerned about is that part I was referring to with regard to Exhibits 781 and 782. I fully accept Mr. Marcussen's statement that they're not going to use 781 and 782. If they're not going to do that, then they should remove from their transcript exhibit all the references to those and the opinions regarding those that are contained beginning at page 7474 in this transcript excerpt. So those would be the two that I'm -- that I'm -- that -- as to which I have particular concern that they should not be admitted because of the -- for the two reasons that I've already mentioned: One, the 65 ter notice; and two, the Court's ruling on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I take it, Mr. Marcussen, the second one's easy to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed. I propose that we identify with Mr. Ackerman the relevant parts and file a notice clarifying precisely what page and line numbers should not be included in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just -- can we do it now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I'll just have to read the passages through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is it document number 3 in your pile? Or is it the next -- is it the next one? No. Mr. Ackerman, I take it it's from line 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually it begins on 7474 at line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh. It's document 4 then, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And finishes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It finishes at line 6 on the next page, 7475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it would be line 4 I think would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Line 4. Is that acceptable, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So by agreement we can exclude or refuse to admit these lines of the transcript and that will save you filing anything. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the question of the 65 ter summary confining the allegation to the activity of paramilitaries and the transcript referring to the army and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this material has been available to the Defence for a long time, both the transcript and the statement. We have found ourselves now in the course of the trial where terms such as "paramilitaries" are given certain interpretations. Now, in our submission it is very difficult when a witness refers to paramilitary and that is put into a statement, and the witness does not use the term "paramilitary" in a specifically technical way, And the witness then later on clarifies that what they mean is, well, police, reserve police, the kind of things that have happened during this trial. This is another example of that. We submit that this -- that evidence like this cannot be excluded on this basis. The Chamber should hear the evidence, hear what the witnesses have to say about the persons they saw on the relevant days, and then make a determination of who they -- who the perpetrators were, if it is at all possible to identify them. In our submission, again we come back to the JCE point. The accused -- if the case ends up being a case solely about Article 7(3) of the Statute, then it might indeed be very relevant whether or not the perpetrators were police or military. For the -- to the extent that we're relying on -- or we end up in a case where the case is about a joint criminal enterprise, ordering and planning, it is our submission that it really doesn't matter. The core of the Prosecution's case is that the accused were members of a joint criminal enterprise with the overall purpose of altering the ethnic balance in Kosovo with a view for the Serbs to hold on to Kosovo. They did so through a number of acts, including the commission of a number of crimes, some of which are charged in the indictment. The way the JCE was executed was that various members of the JCE used structures that they had under their control to have the crimes committed. As long as you're -- as long as the perpetrators on the ground belonged to one of the structures that the Prosecution submits were under the control of one of the accused, all the accused will be responsible in our submission for the crimes committed and charged in the indictment. So we're concerned about this heavy emphasis on definitions used by a witness that are not technical definitions. We take the point that some of this might have been clarified had more investigation been carried out, had more stuff been done, speaking more to the witnesses. But we find ourselves in a situation where the witnesses come to the court and clarify what they meant when they said "paramilitary," and really we submit that such evidence must be admissible and it's important for Your Honours to hear that kind of evidence. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just five seconds more maybe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope it's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it is. Your Honour, this 65 ter notification was given to us very recently. They knew about this testimony in Milosevic since July of 2002. Now, if it was their intention to have this witness testify that what he said in his statement was not correct, that when he talked about paramilitaries he didn't really mean that, that he meant army and police, then we should have been notified of that in the 65 ter. But we're entitled to -- we're entitled to accept when they tell us in the 65 ter that all he's going to talk about is paramilitaries, that that's all he's going to talk about and that they're rejecting what he said in Milosevic. And I think that's a fair position for us to take. I don't think we're required to sit here and guess what they mean in their 65 ter; it has to be precise. And I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a moment to consider the submissions made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We are fairly anxious not to be steeped in history at the conclusion of the evidence in the case and do see force in the general proposition that before evidence of events around 1990 should be led, then it is important to demonstrate the link to the events in 1999. Whether the link's established is a matter to be resolved later in light of the weight we feel we can give to evidence so far removed from the events of 1999 when we look at the whole circumstances. But bearing in mind what's said in the indictment and the submission made by Mr. Marcussen, we do not consider it appropriate to hold this evidence inadmissible. What weight we shall give it in due course is another matter, but we are influenced in this case in particular by the fact that the witness is speaking of events that happened to him personally. So the statement in its entirety we will hold admissible. So far as the first objection taken by Mr. Ackerman is concerned, that is to the late intimation of changes to the transcript, we do not think these are of any real significance in the circumstances and we repel that objection. We would not hold the extracts from the transcript inadmissible on that ground. We are concerned, however, about the way in which the Prosecution have failed to update their case in light of their knowledge since the year 2002 of the evidence that this witness would give. However, we think it is an unrealistic approach to the conduct of this trial to pick our way through the evidence and exclude some explanation that would be necessary to give us a full account of what the witness claims he experienced. And therefore, we do not exclude any part of the transcript, apart from the part excluded by agreement. We remind the Prosecution of their obligation to seek from the Tribunal -- from the Trial Chamber authority to revise the 65 ter statement when there is a significant additional matter to be led in evidence or a significant alteration to be made in the evidence which the witness will present. The Trial Chamber should control that exercise, and there was a failure on this occasion to take that basic step. And in future, failures to comply with our ruling on that will not find favour. If, however, the late notification - because that's a separate matter - the late notification causes foreseeable prejudice to the Defence, then we will accede to any motion that's now made to delay leading of this evidence to enable the 48-hour rule to be complied with and any necessary investigations to be carried out. That would, of course, mean that the witness would have to come back and we would need to proceed now with another witness. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not make such application, but I would like some clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Our practice right now is that if the witness is going to be testifying live and the Prosecution, therefore, is not going to be using a statement or testimony from the Milosevic case, that it's then our obligation if we want to use it to put it into the e-court system, make it an exhibit, notify the Prosecution, and do all those things that are in the order to be able to use it. Now, if it's the position of the Chamber that the statement of the witness and the transcript from Milosevic is automatically available to everybody for use during examination of the witness without notice, then that would save us an extraordinary amount of time. But we had absolutely no notice that the statement of Milosevic -- the Milosevic trial transcript was going to be used during this witness's testimony, none, zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll ask the Prosecution their position on this because it may be that this is a procedure that could be followed. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Mr. Hannis just explained that the Defence was put on notice yesterday afternoon about the use of the excerpts from the Milosevic transcripts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, but we're dealing now with a particular question and it's a question of general application. If what the Defence seek to use is the previous statement made in the -- in evidence in the Milosevic trial by a witness who's going to be here, is there any need for compliance with the rule at moment that they include on a list as soon as a witness commences his evidence the transcript as a potential exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We would submit that, yes, it might be a formality, but I think it is important for us to know what statements the Defence intend to use for the purpose of cross-examination. Furthermore, there might be an issue of whether or not the entire transcript or, for that matter, statement becomes an exhibit or whether it only should be the portions of the statement or transcript that have been put to the witness during cross-examination. So I would submit that we should keep the rule as it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the last point is one that would be dealt with on a case-by-case basis and doesn't really address the issue. I think as presently advised we should adhere to the present -- the rule that was made, Mr. Ackerman, and -- but I leave it to you to draw to our attention any particular difficulty you're experiencing in complying with the rule. But at the moment, I don't think I would like to jump to the point where preparation could be rendered more chaotic than it is at the moment. And I have another comment to make about that before concluding. There is one other matter also to be dealt with, and that is the objection you take to the individual exhibits, which are referred to in the statement. Whether or not you are correct I think can only be determined when we've seen them and heard what the witness has to say about them. So the question of whether they're exhibited can be dealt with at the end of his evidence now that we're alerted to that being a potential bone of contention between the parties. The final general point I wish to make is to the Prosecution and that is that better preparation of this case is going to save a great deal of time. We've now used an hour and five minutes of today's hearing dealing with an issue which would have been dealt with in a different way if notification of all of the material to be used with a witness was made more timeously. Now, I know the explanation that you will offer in response being the changes to the arrangement for the attendance of witnesses that had been made. I'm afraid there's going to have to be a bit more thought given to the planning of witnesses' attendance and preparing them so that this situation doesn't arise again so far as it can be avoided. Now, Mr. Ackerman, is there something else you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully accept the Prosecution's position that we should notify them if we're going to use the transcript from Milosevic or excerpts therefrom. Why then are they not required to notify us? I mean, that just doesn't -- that's not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope I've made it clear that that won't happen again. It will be up to them to make an application to alter the 65 ter statement, and I think I made it clear that a failure to do that will not be met sympathetically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this is a one-time pass.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in the circumstances of this witness where there has been a measure of uncertainty about the timing because of other decisions that have arisen, we are allowing it. But I was taking the opportunity to make it clear that the position will be different in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So now, please, can we have Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: While we wait, I should maybe just follow usual good practice of stating what paragraphs in the indictment this testimony is relevant to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The evidence of this witness is particularly relevant to paragraphs 72(d), 75(d), 77(d), Schedule D to the indictment circumstantially, and paragraph 88 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Berisha, this Trial Chamber already has before it a great deal of the information that you have on the matters on which you are being asked to give evidence. We have a written statement, we have supplementary information bringing the statement up-to-date, we have parts of the written transcript of the evidence you gave in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. So we have a lot of material which we have already read. The reason for the hearing today is to enable counsel for the Prosecution and for the accused to ask you questions, either to add to the information, to clarify things, or to challenge what you've said. And because we have so much and we want to get as much as we can, it's important that you concentrate on the particular questions that are asked of you, and try to confine your answers to the point that the question relates to so that we get as much new information as possible. We don't want to go over again, unless we have to, but we'll try to avoid as much as possible going over again the information you've already given. The first person to ask questions will be for the Prosecution, and that is Mr. Marcussen. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 17th of August, 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think 2001, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do indeed stand corrected. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, over the last two days have you had a chance to read the Albanian translation of that statement?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you bring -- did you notice a few things in that statement that you wished to be corrected?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Only on two or three places I had to make some corrections; it referred to some dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is it correct that in -- there is mention in paragraph 2 of your statement of the Directorate of Civil Defence. That should have been the popular defence?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, it was the Secretariat of Popular Defence, not of civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And also in the fifth paragraph of your statement, that is the fifth paragraph of page 2 of the English; the first paragraph on page 3 of the B/C/S; and the second paragraph on the third page of the Albanian translation, there is mention that on the 25th of March, members of the Kuci family passed by your house. That should have been the Berisha family. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, the Berisha family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And finally, there was a correction to the first paragraph on page 4 of the English version; the third paragraph on page 4 of the B/C/S version; and the second paragraph on page 5 of the Albanian version which relates to your brother going to -- towards Albania in the -- via Prizren and returning. And you reiterated that the corrections you had made in the Milosevic trial to that passage was the correct one. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, except for those corrections, is the rest of the statement a correct reflection of your recollection of the events as they occurred at the time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. Everything is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We would be tendering then -- we have discussed it earlier, but we will be tendering then P2326 as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, also when you met with representatives of the Prosecution were you shown a number of excerpts from your testimony in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: We are not getting the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The exhibit number, Mr. Marcussen, I think it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Is it for the transcript or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Or for the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's for the original statement. It's P2326 and it's to complete the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, was -- were the excerpts of the transcript read back to you and translated into Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And did you make some corrections to the transcript?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Only two or three corrections about things that were incorrect in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And this morning have you seen a copy of the transcripts where those corrections had been -- has been written in, in hand?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, those corrections having been made, do the excerpts of the transcript reflect your recollection of the events as they occurred?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, as I have described them they are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, then I would like to tender P2325 as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, as the President pointed out to you, the Chamber and the Defence have had an opportunity to read both your statement and the excerpts of your testimony in the Milosevic case thoroughly and they are well aware of the contents of your evidence. So I will only be going over a few points with a view to clarify some issues, and then I'll be asking you some questions about documents that were attached to your statement. But really, we're just trying to clarify some specific points in this regard. You explain in your statement that you had been given a pistol when you became mayor.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was the purpose of giving you that pistol?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I was issued the pistol for my personal protection, and it was a property of the secretariat of the interior, not my personal property. It was an official pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I understand your evidence to be that the pistol was taken away from you again in August of 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On 5th of August, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, absolutely correct. I'm the one making the mistakes here today. In August 1990 had there been changes in the political situation that led to the request that you return the pistol?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: In 1990 big changes occurred. The authority of the local authorities fell, and the authority of police increased in Suhareke municipality. And at that time everything was in the hands of the police and not in the hands of the president of the municipality. Therefore, on 5th of August, 1990, in the courtyard of the municipality they had prepared a group of young men to be sent for recruitment in Nis. At that time, three policemen came wearing vests, anti-bullet vests, and they submitted me a summons to report to the commander of the police who had come from Belgrade in order to hand over my official pistol. And it is then when I realised that the authority was in the hands of the police and no longer in the hands of the municipal authorities. So the role of the president of the municipality decreased, and the role of the police increased and the police actually took over everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: If you allow me, for this -- what happened, I informed the Secretariat of People's Defence in Pristina, Slobodan Bojic, that is to say for the case of my pistol being returned. He just said that he would look into this matter, but that was only in words and nothing else happened. He was a colonel by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. There's another issue that I'd like to clarify. On the 5th of April, 1991, when you were dismissed from the office, I understand that you knew two of the people who came to your office, but there were three security officers, state security officers you say, that were with them. Did you know the three security officers?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So how come you know that they were from state security?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Some clerks in the Municipal Assembly recognised them, and they told me that they were officers of the Serbian State Security, while two others for clerks in the Municipal Assembly and they handed over me the decision adopted by the Assembly for the dismissal of the Albanian workers, which we found injust because we were elected -- I was elected by the members -- the delegates of the Suhareke Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. You say they handed over to you the decision adopted by the Assembly for the dismissal of the Albanian workers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Serbian Assembly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It bears the date 4th of April, 1991, and on 5th of April, they came to my office and told me to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Halit Berisha, how many people lived in Suva Reka town at that time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: At that time it had about 50 to 60.000 inhabitants, and as for the origin about 95 per cent were Albanians and the other 5 per cent were Romas and other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were the other 5 per cent primarily Romas, as the transcript say, or were they primarily Serb?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Mostly Serb and about 2 to 300 Romas. As for Serbs, they were about 3.400.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And for the whole of the municipality, of the municipality of Suva Reka, how many people lived there?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: At that time, approximately 60.000 people lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in Suva Reka town itself, just the urban part of Suva Reka, how many people lived there?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: At that time the Suhareke town had about 8.000 inhabitants. We were not able to have the exact statistics because the 1991 census was not carried out in Kosova. So we did not have the exact number of the population in Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to now put Exhibit P615, page 52 on the monitor, please. And could we give it one twist to the left, please, so we get it turned horizontally? That should have been to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that clockwise or anti-clockwise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Clockwise. We're zooming in I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Turn it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And let's try to zoom in just one more time and see how that looks. Right. Could we move it up -- well, could we move the picture down a bit. Oh, sorry, you're seeing it -- the result I would like to obtain is that we get a bit more of the -- where the two roads are meeting, the two red roads, I'd like to be able to see as well, but I'd like us to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Halit Berisha, can you see the map clearly on your screen?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we'll need the assistance of the usher just to do a few marks on the -- on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You describe in your statement that on the 24th of March of -- maybe before, but there were a number of strategic positions occupied by snipers of the police or the military. You mentioned that there were snipers in the post office building. Where on this map is the post office building?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: First of all, this is the road from Pristina to Prizren. The red line here, just on the red line itself, is the police station. And in front of the police station there were two rocket-launchers positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, let's just do first the positions that I mentioned. If we could indicate where the post office is, please.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, the post office is here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, it's not rocket-launchers, it's mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Halit Berisha, you just made a dot. Could you put an A at that place where the post office is.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And now that you have marked where the police station is, maybe just so that it's clear on the transcript what we're talking about, could you put a B where -- sorry, where the police station is.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. So A is the post office, B is the police station. You also mentioned that --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- there was a position in the bell-tower. Where is that on the map, if you first can make a dot and then put a C next to it.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The tower that we mentioned is at the clinic which is approximately here. This is the tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could you put a C like Charlie at that point.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a few more dots to make. I don't know whether you want to break now or whether we should do it when we're finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's finish the map and then we'll break off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Halit Berisha, I think in your transcript in the Milosevic case you indicate that there were also a position close to the winery. Where is that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question -- oh, yes. It is here, the winery is here. All this here is the winery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Please put a D at that place underneath the dot you just made.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I think you also have mentioned that there was a position at the -- at the old post office. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The old post office is somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If you could make -- put an E like Eric or echo at that place.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And were there any other positions where there were snipers stationed that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. This is where the Balkan Hotel is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And would you put a -- we have reached an F like fox-trot.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Are those -- are those the sniper positions you are aware of in Suva Reka town?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now while we have the map on the screen, could you indicate where your house was?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: My house was here, right behind the post office. Somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you put a G like George at that place?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then finally could I ask you to indicate where the mosque was.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The mosque was here. This is where the house is, approximately here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if you would put an H there, please, like hotel.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think we need two lines a bit -- the lower part of the H is very difficult for me to see on the screen, just so we have the record clear later on.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I propose that we take the break here and then we'll resume afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But I would like to make this an exhibit maybe before, I'm reminded kindly by our court officer. We'll make this an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC40, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at ten past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you say in your statement that on the 28th of March you -- excuse me. I'll go a little back. I'm on the wrong page. My apologies, Mr. Berisha. On the 25th of March a number of family members, 20 to 30 family members from the Berisha and the Ramadan Berisha family passed by your house, and you say in your statement that they told you that people had been killed and robbed near their houses and they were fleeing from the Serbs. Did you see yourself the people that they were fleeing from?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, 1999, at about 6.00 in the morning, myself and my brother Jashar were in our courtyard where at that time our cousins from the other side of the street, they were leaving. Some were still in their slippers, and they told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The question -- the question is very specific. Did you see the people from whom they were fleeing? It's either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, now Mr. Marcussen will ask you more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw those people, and they were leaving because of the Serbian army and the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did you yourself see the people you describe as the Serbian army and the Serbian police? Could you see them?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I saw the people who were leaving, but I did not see the police. But they told me, the people who were leaving told me that they were leaving because of the Serbian police and army. They were very scared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you remember that they described the people they were fleeing from as members of the police and the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's getting pretty leading. I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: He just answered: Saw them leave because of the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why do you ask the question? I mean, it's a very, very leading question surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I withdraw. I can -- I am fine with the record as it stands. We can leave it as it is. So I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I'll jump ahead in time in your statement, and I'll -- would like to ask some questions about the 26th of March, 1999. You say in your statement that your brother on the morning of the 26th of March, 1999, went to the petrol station where he worked. Do you remember what he was wearing that day?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: He was manager of the petrol station, Beopetrol, he went to work at about 8.00. He had a jacket with "Beopetrol" written on the back. He had a jumper, multi-coloured jumper inside. He also was wearing jeans and sneakers, red sneakers. Underneath he had some long underwear with white and red stripes. I had a similar pair myself, that's why I know. At that night only myself and my wife stayed at home. All the rest of the family had left home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was your brother also in your house that night?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. On the night of the 25th to the 26th of March, yes, he was in the same room with me, sleeping in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And how do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, could you tell us again what he was wearing under his jeans.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He had jeans, but under them he had track-suit -- bottom part of the track-suit, but also some underwear which was long-Johns with stripes, red and white. It was very cold; that's why he was wearing so many clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What was the colour of the track-suit if you remember or the bottom of the track-suit?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The -- they were blue, blue, jeans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the -- and the -- you just explained to Judge Bonomy that he was wearing the bottom part of a track-suit and then he was wearing some long underwear. But the track-suit, do you remember the colour of that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. The jacket was blue and on the back of the jacket there were -- there was the word "Beopetrol" because their enterprise was called like that, their company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe we'll get back to that. I don't know if there's a translation issue, but did you -- since -- since the 26th of March, have you seen any of your brother's clothes again?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Some of his clothes I was able to see sometime in July 1999, after I came back from Albania in the mass grave between Prizren and Suhareke. It's Kroj i Popit, the place is called Kroj i Popit, and at the place of the exhumation we found many things. Among other things we found part of his leg and we could see the clothes that he was wearing underneath. We also found things belonging to other people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to show Exhibit P133, page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And while we wait for that to come up, are you aware of whether a photograph was taken of the clothes that you identified at the exhumation site?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It's not this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could I ask that this photograph be turned anti-clockwise, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, just wait a minute, please. Now, on this photograph do you see the piece of clothing that you identified?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can you -- there are numbers on the different items on the photograph. Could you read the number of the item that you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: KRA 1072, that belonged to my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The other things belonged to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berisha, have you also given a blood sample to a forensic team?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. My brother Eqrim and my sister Aziza gave a blood sample for identification. And in September I was informed by the forensic medical team at UNMIK that my brother was identified in the mass grave of Batajnica at Belgrade. The last victims were returned on the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I will again ask the Judges and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, which year was that, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That the blood sample was given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, the identification of his brother's body at Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I will have to look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would have to find the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm not answering this question at this moment. Maybe Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, you said you were told in September that your brother had been identified in a gave at Batajnica. September in which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The UNMIK office informed me. It's the current year, 2006, September 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I would now like to turn to the events on the 26th of March, 1999. You described in your statement how you heard an explosion and then you saw the minaret being -- having been destroyed. We need a bit more details about that. Now, first of all when you heard the explosion, where were you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It wasn't the 26th of March, it was the 28th of March, 1999. It was Bajram, which is a Muslim holiday, and at 11.55 a.m. I was in my courtyard when I heard a big explosion. And normally I could see the minaret from my courtyard, but from that moment on I couldn't see it anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, from -- from your courtyard can you see the whole mosque or only part of the mosque?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The minaret. It was a tall building. It was about 45 metres tall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you had heard the explosion, I understand you called a neighbour to inquire about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did they -- had -- did they tell you who they -- had they seen what had caused the explosion?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: There is a family there called Elshani and they live very close to the mosque, and they had seen the explosion and the collapse of the minaret. Fortunately it did not fall on to their house; it fell on the other side, so it did not cause any damage to their house. At that time they had seen a vehicle of the army, a gazika, in camouflage colours. It was a red vehicle. That was the only car that moved at that time. It went in the direction of Birac and it was a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did they tell you whether they had seen any persons getting in or out of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, it was those people who saw them because they lived very close to where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did they describe the people they saw? In order, did they say what they looked like, whether they were in uniform, for example?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: They saw the soldiers in uniforms and the blowing up of the minaret, and they were scared because of that big explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Another point of clarification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you move on from -- is this a clarification that exists in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It partly exists in the transcript, but I'm not sure that it's clear from the transcript that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When he says he rang a relative in the statement, is it now -- is the evidence now different or is this an elaboration of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think it's only an elaboration of the evidence; that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, is -- are the Elshani family related to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
