utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, my cousin is married in that family --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Elshani family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You -- you have also mentioned in your statement that later on in the day you were told by a Serb policeman that you should go to Albania or you would be killed. I understand from the transcript in the Milosevic case that at the time you gave the statement the name of this police officer wasn't recorded, but in the Milosevic case you did remember his name. What was the name of this person?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, he was a reservist policeman, Novic, Radovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: He wore a police uniform because I could tell the colours of the police uniforms, because they were blue, while the army uniforms were green.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The uniform he was wearing on that day, was it -- was it blue or different kinds of blues? Was there a pattern on it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It was blue. While the dominating colour was blue, but it was camouflage, it had a pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before you saw Djura on that day, did you already know that he was a reserve police officer?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Well, I knew that because he was a neighbour and I knew him very well, and everybody in my family knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would like if we could see Exhibit P1807.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, this is the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And could we see the second page of this exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the minaret which was blown up and collapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, once again I'll jump in your evidence and I'll ask you about a person you saw on the -- you say in your statement that you saw on the -- on the 16th of May, 1999. In your statement he is described as Misko Nisavic. What position did he have?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Which -- what --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: His name was Nisavic, Milorad, and his pseudonym was Misko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I knew him personally. And on the 15th of May, some members of my family were staying at a house when the police came and surrounded them. And the police notified him. He came to this house, and he told that they had to come to report at the municipality. He recognised my son, and he told him that I had to report as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. This officer that you reported to, what part of the police did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: State security of Serbia or Yugoslavia, as it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I understand from your -- your statement and the Judges on the defence, we have this as well, that you were not harmed and you were allowed to leave shortly after that, and you explained in your statement how there would be a humanitarian organisation that would come. Now, on the 21st of May, 1999, you described that six members of the police came to your home and you mention Andrejevic as being a police officer that you knew and you had 15 minutes to leave to Albania and you would -- now, this person, did you know him before this particular event?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, this happened on the 21st of May, 1999, at about 10.00, 10.00 a.m. when Andrejevic came, Sinisa Andrejevic. He is the son of Andjelija and Miodrag Andrejevic. They were teachers. They came to the house where we were staying which was my aunt's house and they told us that you have to get ready in 15 minutes and go to Albania and you will never see this land again. I knew him. He was wearing a police uniform, blue, and they were armed. They had Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So before this event you knew him and you knew that he was a police officer. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him and his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Then you explain in your statement how you subsequently left with the convoy. Those who didn't have their transport themselves, there were buses and two trucks. You left for Albania and you explain how your identity papers were taken away from you. And then you explain that you -- well, you were for a while in Albania in a refugee camp, and then you returned to Kosovo. Now, there's a slight -- I think we need to clarify, although it's not so important to your evidence. But there are two different dates for when you returned. One is the 23rd of June, 1999, and the other is the 13th of June, 1999. Which one is correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, I went back on the 23rd of June, 1999. It was 8.00 in the morning when I got home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like -- when you came back, you have explained that you started -- you took up a function in the municipal building again on the 8th of October, 1999. And you -- you then collected some documents. I'd like to talk about that for a little bit. First off -- excuse me, just one minute. Now, you provided a list of documents to us. Where did you find those documents?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 8th of October, 1999, -- before that there was an administrator of UNMIK who was in charge of setting up a board that would manage the commune, and I was part of that. I was given the office of Stanislav Andjelkovic, the former mayor, and I found in that office most of the documents -- all of the documents that I have brought here, most of the documents I found in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you describe to us -- you say you found them. Where in the office were they placed?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: There were some drawers and I found them in the drawers. I found the documents, I put them in order -- I found other documents as well, not only the ones that I've brought here. I photocopied these and I gave them to the Tribunal because I thought they were useful in explaining the events that happened after 1991, after I was dismissed from my job, to the day when they left the offices of the municipality in -- on the 10th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So you yourself took the documents from the drawer? It was not brought to you by anybody else; it was yourself who found them there?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: There was one document about the number of the soldiers; that was found in a floppy disk and it was brought to my office to print out. That document was brought to me, that floppy was brought to me; the other documents I found myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Have you -- have you changed anything in those documents?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And from the time that you collected them and -- to the time when you gave them to the Office of the Prosecutor, did you have them in your custody all the time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, I kept them in my custody, except the document where you can find the telephone number of -- my telephone, my brother's telephone number, that was found on a calendar, and that is in my handwriting. The original is at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then when you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, you handed these documents over to the investigator who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. The investigator saw the original and took the photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you some questions about some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And I think if we could get P778 on the screen, please. There we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could I ask you to read the title of this document. I believe it says: "The Government of Serbia," and so on, the part that's in the middle.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. This is in Serbian. If you would like me to translate them, it's addressed to the Government of Serbia, and the operational body of the Republic of Serbia for Kosovo and Metohija. This was addressed to the Suhareke branch on the 28th of March, 1991. The number is 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can scroll a bit further down on the document, please, a bit further down. That was -- a bit up so we can see number 1 being Halit Berisha and then the remainder of the names if you could do that. Just go a little bit up. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berisha, you see here -- I understand this is a document for the proposal of the replacement of a number of people in the municipal authorities of Suva Reka and we see now on the screen a list of people beginning with your name and listing eight people. Now, my question is: The people listed here, are they -- are they Albanian or Serbian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The people listed here are Albanian, and there are two others who are listed as secretaries of the secretariat, but they were secretaries of the people's defence. But they were not removed. The request referred only to the Albanian workers, and all the names listed from 1 to 8, they were all dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then we can see at the bottom of the page Dr. Bobek Vuksanovic?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What ethnicity was he, Serb or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Bobek Vuksanovic is the son of Ymer Shetra who was Albanian and his mother is Serbian. He's an illegitimate child. His parents were not married. He was born outside the wedlock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was he considered by people in Suva Reka as being Serb or Albanian or neither or?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: He was regarded as a Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He bears the last name of his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There are four -- there are five more people listed here in number 2 through 6.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: They're all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Might I interrupt? As to the first page, I'd like to ask the witness a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could the first page be shown again and could the witness be asked to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Halit Berisha, do you see the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't have the -- we have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Is it being given to the witness in a language which he understands?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's the Serbian version. I believe he understands Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He understands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Under Belgrade where it says as at a meeting, there are some circumstances listed as the reason for dismissal. Do you have anything to say concerning those circumstances? Did they in fact exist or not? That's what I want to know from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Bosnian Serb, there is a reference to -- to --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The only reason was because I was Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There's reference to something that is described in the English translation as the well-known -- as well-known incidents, support for the Kacanik constitution. Could you explain to the court what that was.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It is the Kacanik constitution. It's not about the discriminating laws that were adopted by Serbia against the Albanian population. And this was done on purpose so that we Albanians were dismissed and they took up their positions in Suhareke. This was the only reason. It is true that on the 7th of September -- it is true that on the 7th of September the Kacanik constitution was adopted in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you like me to explore this further, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: If you're able to, subject to the leave of the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's meaningless at the moment. It needs to be explored.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you explain what that constitution was, please.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The constitution was adopted by the legitimate delegates of Kosova, who before the 2nd of July, 1990, came out with the constitutional declaration. And it was adopted in front of the parliament building because they were prevented of going inside the parliament. So the legitimate delegate of the Albanian people in Kosova adopted this constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Who prevented them from going inside the parliament building?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The police, the Serbian police, on 2nd of July, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was the -- was the constitution that was adopted by the parliament was that seen as unconstitutional --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Was the constitution that was adopted on that day, was that seen as unconstitutional by the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The Serbian authorities did not recognise it and considered it unconstitutional, but it was constitutional in the view of the Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Marcussen, if you want to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could we have the next exhibit up which is P779. And just for the assistance of the registry staff, I think we'll try to go through the list that I provided you now so you can prepare the list one. I think we can stick to the list we provided at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you read the title of this document, please, the underlined part.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I will translate it. It's a request by legitimate representatives of the Serbian people in the territory of Suhareke municipality. This is the title of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then would you read, please, or translate for me the first sentence in the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: "The weapons of the Territorial Defence which are stored in the warehouse of the Territorial Defence in Djinovce village should immediately be distributed to the Serbian people in the territory of Suhareke municipality. The surplus, if any, should be stored in Balkan premises and other ammunitions, such as hand-grenades, rifle grenades, and mines to be distributed as well."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. So this is a document for the distribution of weapons only to the Serb population in Suva Reka. Is that your understanding of the document?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There is no dates, I believe, on this document. Could you help us. When did you think -- when do you think approximately this document dates from, if you can help us?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Approximately in late 1989 or beginning of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And why do you think that is so? I don't know if you get -- got my translation through. Why do you think it dates from around that time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Because approximately around that time they began to arm the Serbian population. We had only one road that divided us, our family, from them, and we had knowledge that they were being armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so when you say "they," are -- is that --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I mean the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could show Exhibit P780. And if we could turn that clockwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What is this, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: This is a list of persons, Serbs, of their villages, and at the bottom of the list there is a pseudonym, Roma. It refers to Roma and Koljaci, meaning slayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we scroll down to the bottom of the page and out to the -- to the right part of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- this is what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: These are the names of the villages in Suhareke municipality, Mushtishte, Suhareke itself, Delani, Leshani, and in the end is listed Ilic Srecko, the commander of this unit. He was born in Leshan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think you already said it but the names on this list are they Serb or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: All of them are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we move on to the next one, 7 -- P781, please. Now, again, this we need to turn anti-clockwise. Okay, we don't need to zoom on this I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, can you see the names on this page, please?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, they're all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And are the names -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then if we could go to Exhibit P784.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me just a moment, I don't know what Mr. Marcussen's doing with P781, but he told us earlier he had no intention of introducing 781 or 782 when I made an objection to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, that is correct. And I wonder whether -- can we go back -- no, I take that point and this was a mistake on my part, I think. Could we go back and see 781, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's easy, you don't need to see it. We refused to admit it earlier, so it's refused admission --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll ignore the part of the transcript from 59, 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: No, I apologise to Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: 784, please, if we could see that. If we can zoom in on the actual text a bit on this one. We can leave it as it is there. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What does the title -- what does the first three lines of this document say after the number beginning K20 --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The civilian defence staff of the Suhareke municipality. All of them are Serbs. And second is -- under 2 is Mushtishte it's a village in Suhareke municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You say all the people on the list are Serbs. You had a chance to review this list when we met today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Under 7, Ndrec Lalaj, member of the civilian defence, so he was Albanian by nationality but he was engaged in these units of the civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Then I think -- is it possible to zoom out a little bit so we can see all the names on -- can we have something in between?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, of the names that you are see now on the monitor --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: -- how come the person you just mentioned as being Albanian. Are there any other Albanian names there?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please, of this exhibit. And can we zoom in again on the text, if we can capture it all that will be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: On this one, are the names --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, there are no Albanians on this one; only Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And if we can do the next page of this exhibit and do the same zooming exercise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this one all of them are Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to then go to Exhibit P785, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, that is, as I understand it, a document from the Balkan factory in Suva Reka and it's dated the 10th of April, 1992. We have the translation, so I don't think we need to go through that, but it's about distribution of weapons to employees at the factory. The question I have for you, Mr. Berisha, is: To your knowledge in 1992, were the employees at the factory, were they Serb or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: As of in or about 8 or 9 August, 1990, the Albanians were dismissed and they were no longer working in the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could now go to Exhibit P786, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There's an awful lot of things crammed in on this page. I think it's -- do you recognise this document from the documents that you gave us to --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, this is the Official Gazette. It's about the change of names of schools bearing Albanian names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So by this decision the names of Albanian -- of schools in Suva Reka municipality were changed from Albanian names to other names. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now I'd like to call up P787.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There's a decision I believe beginning in the first column, and that's a decision on the managerial organs of the cultural institute in Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The cultural institutes, and it was named after Jovan Jovanovic Zmaj and all the members of this group were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Then we will go to P788, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is a document for the setting up of -- it's about the municipality counsel and verification of the mandate of councillors. And there's a list of 27 councillors that have been verified. Are they Serb or Albanian, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we can zoom in on the names if you need to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of 27 members of the Assembly that was established at that time, all of them were Serbs, although the proportion ratio in the population was 95 per cent Albanian and 5 per cent Serbs and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like now to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The previous one which was P787, which number is it on the list in the statement -- page 5 of the English version of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It is also -- it's number 8. There are a number of decisions under 8, but they have been given two separate exhibit numbers here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we could now move to Exhibit P789. If we can zoom in on the bottom left quarter of this page, please. A little out from here, but otherwise we are fine. What I think we can do with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Halit Berisha, we are seeing here I think a list of electoral districts in the municipality of Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, it is a list of electoral units composed by them. For example, they divided Suva Reka into five electoral units and they did the same with the village of Mushtishte, and, below there, seven, eight, nine, ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You say "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The Serbs who were in power at that time, and they divided these electoral units not on the basis of number of inhabitants but only to be able to create that list we just saw with this 27 candidates on it. For example, here at number 6 you have Grejkovce, Dubravce, Selograzde, Stavrovo. In this area more than 5.000 inhabitants --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can I stop you just so we are clear about what this evidence shows. So under number 6 there is a list of villages in Suva Reka municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you are saying to the best of your knowledge in that -- in those villages together there were more than 5.000 inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Approximately, in all the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Together. Thank you. Yes. And if we now look, for example, at the electoral districts number 12 and 13, Bujani 1 and 2. How many people lived in Bujani?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The village of Dvorane had approximately 300 inhabitants and it was divided into two zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Were -- in Dvorane, were the inhabitants mainly Serb or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Majority was Serb. Only some families were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And in the -- in the -- in the seven villages listed under item 6, electorate district 6, were the inhabitants mainly Albanian or Serb?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Only Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And what did you say -- why do you think the electoral districts were made this way?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Only to be able to create the list of 27 candidates for the municipality of Suhareke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the date of that -- what's the -- Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would -- this is exactly the type of the evidence what -- what we were objecting about. And this will definitely take us into 2009 with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm very surprised that the Prosecution have time to spend on this, but that's their choice at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And my learned colleague has elicited the answer from the witness which is really for an expert witness. I don't see how the witness can answer such a question, that this witness can answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anyway, I would like to know the date of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That I can probably assist from the translation. Can we look up at the top of this page, please, out in the right-hand corner. We'll need a bit further out to the right. We don't seem to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I cannot see it very clearly. It's 29th of April, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know what year it is?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I cannot see the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Do you know from -- do you happen to know what year this was?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It should be 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And maybe if we scroll down on this page. In the same view we have -- if we stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Am I correct that out in the right-hand column, just about in the middle, we have reference to a decision taken on the 29th of April, 2000 -- 1992, Mr. Berisha?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like to -- we have two more exhibits to go. I just need to pass a message to my -- oh, no, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could we call up P790, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, this is a decision of the Red Cross in Kosovo from 24 October 1991. It's about the replacement of the secretary of the Red Cross Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Can we zoom in so we can see paragraphs 1 and 2 of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ahmed Krasniqi was dismissed and Ilic Krsto was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Krasniqi, was he --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Krasniqi was Albanian and the latter is Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the last document I'd like us to go to is P794. It is a document from the 11th of May, 1999, about the creation of a committee to assess war damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If we can scroll down a bit so we can see the names of members of the committee listed in -- yeah, I think this is a fine view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The number of members of the committee listed there, Mr. Berisha, are they Serb or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: They're all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender the following exhibits that we have been discussing today. We've already been through some of them, but we'd like to have P133, P1807 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what -- hold on until I find these items. P133 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I believe that was the -- that was a picture with the track-suit identified by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no issue over that. Yes, on you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: P1807 is the picture --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no issue over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And then the exhibits that I've been going through here in the last bits of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And they are just to mention the numbers and we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've got a note of the numbers, so you don't need to go through them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we need to hear what's to be said against that, since objection was taken. Now, have you any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. It's -- just to clarify, my case manager asked me to make sure that we have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, my case manager -- maybe we might as well clarify this. Would Your Honours like us to replace P2325, that is the transcripts where we have agreed that a certain portion should be stricken or can we leave the record as it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions at this stage. In re-direct maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berisha, one thing I would like to be clear about before we go any further. You told us that you were advised in September of this year that your brother, Jashar Berisha's body had been found in a mass grave at Batajnica. You also told us that the item of clothing had been recovered from a mass grave between Prizren and Suva Reka at a place called Kroj i Popit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The massacre of the 26th of March of 1999 occurred from 12.00 a.m. -- p.m. to 2.30 p.m. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I haven't asked you a question yet. Would you just hold on, please. When was it that the item of clothing was recovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The clothing was found sometime in July 1999 when we returned from Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you -- did you personally find it in the grave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Myself, my wife, and Hyseni Berisha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll follow the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm wondering if I may just intervene here to make a request, and perhaps Mr. O'Sullivan could assist us here. We have a witness here to follow. He arrived I am told around midnight or after midnight and he has complained about being very exhausted. I don't think, but I want to confirm, that there's no need for him to remain here and perhaps come into court just for a few minutes completely nackered. I don't know if perhaps you could release him to return tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to say how long the cross-examination will be. Can you, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, I can't say, Your Honour, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, tell me the order first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we'll follow the indictment, and I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Fila. Can you give me --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have some questions, Your Honour, very few, but I would just like to clarify matters rather than ask questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you embark on that, who has a substantial number of questions for this witness? Well, I think the witness that you have in waiting better wait for the moment, Mr. Stamp. Carry on, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Berisha, I am Toma Fila and I am Defence counsel for Nikola Sainovic. I will ask you very briefly about certain matters just to clarify them. There are some things I find sort of strange. If a few days ago -- in September of this year you received information about your brother in Batajnica, did you take over your brother's body? As far as I know the identification was carried out a long time ago. It's a bit strange that it happened just now, isn't it? The question is: Did you take over your brother's body?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, he's in the morgue in Pristina because we requested that the whole of the victims of the Berisha family be together for a funeral, for a proper funeral. We're still expecting 31 people, 31 bodies to come. I have still not received the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to clarify this because as far as I know the identification was carried out a long time ago. Please don't misunderstand me. I'm just asking you this to clarify matters. Further on, P0789 that the Prosecution dealt with, you talked about electoral units that Suva Reka was broken up into several subunits, but you have this same decision on the appointment of the municipal electoral commission, the assemblymen of the municipality of Suva Reka. Since this is a document that you brought in, and as far as I know you know it by heart, as far as I can see it's Albanians on the commission; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't have this document before me. They were appointed by the Serbs, by the Serb authorities. They were not part of the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please have it returned. No problem. Could we have it back on your screens P00789, an exhibit that you showed, it was the one but last.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could all microphones please be switched off except for the speaker's. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object, this document P00789. It's the one that's here right now. Now, could we have a look at the right-hand side of this document. That's it, isn't it? Could the right-hand side -- the bottom, rather, be enlarged, on the right-hand side but the bottom. Yes. Yes, a bit more, a bit more. Yes. Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please read this. Miodrag Plazenic [phoen] is a Serb, but what about Avdi Gashi, Judge Avdi Gashi. What is he by ethnicity, Albanian or Serb?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Avdi Gashi and Rustem Hasani did not take part in the commission. Their names are there but I know for sure that they did not park -- take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I'm just asking you what it says in this decision, that they are being appointed members of the commission, and then further on you have Lalaj Ndrec, is he also an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm saying that they are Albanian, but they did not take part in the workings of the commission. They resigned. They resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about that. They were appointed members of the commission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Would you slow down for a moment and observe some break between your question and the witness's answer so that there's time for the translation to be completed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to take you back to your statement, paragraph 2. You said that you were appointed on the 24th of May, 1989, as president for Suva Reka. Who actually organised the elections where you were elected?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The election occurred earlier. I was made mayor after the elections in the commune of Suva Reka. The Assembly of Kosovo organised the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who organised the elections? That is my question. Then you said on the 5th of April, 1991, five Serbs came in, three of which were from the secret service and two from the Serbian Assembly. What Serbian Assembly is this that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: A decision is missing here. Of the Serbian Assembly because this is a request of the socialist party and this is a decision of the Serbian Assembly to dismiss people. I have this decision here. It was a decision of the Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question you're being asked is: Which Serbian Assembly? Just concentrate -- can you tell us which --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just give me short answers and then we'll be done quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Fila a moment. Mr. Berisha, just look at me, please. Mr. Berisha, look at me. Which Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Assembly of Serbia, the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. One document is missing in this bunch of documents, and I have it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you understand the answers --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that we are not understanding each other. I understand the answer but that's not what I asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Are you claiming that Boban Vuksanovic was a member of the Serbian Assembly of -- the Assembly of Serbia in Belgrade? Bobek Vuksanovic?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you have your own statement? Could you please look at paragraph 2 in your own statement? Yes. And you will see here that five people came, three from state security, two Serbs from the Serb Assembly. What Serb Assembly were you referring to? That's my question, Bobek and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I may. It's being suggested that the witness is confused because he's referring to a Serb Assembly in Belgrade I think. The statement is quite clear. It says, "Vuksanovic was a member of -- was the secretary of the Serbian Assembly in Suva Reka." That is what it's saying in the English version of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question that's being asked. The question relates to a person called Boban Vuksanovic and what Mr. Fila wants to know which Serb Assembly it is said he is from. Now, is there anything wrong with that question? Hold on, hold on, hold on. The problem, Mr. Fila, with your involvement throughout this trial is that you get -- you want to speak before the answer had been completed. I understand your anxiety to make progress; in fact, I commend it. But it can in the end of the day it can slow things down. We have a Scottish expression, the more hurry, the less speed. So perhaps if we just take this calmly we'll get there a bit more quickly. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The witness has said that the decision was issued by the Serbian Assembly of the Republic of Serbia. The statement says that Vuksanovic was the secretary of the Serbian Assembly of Suva Reka. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the statement says that Borisavljevic was the secretary of the Serb Assembly in Suva Reka. We're not asking about him. We're earlier in the statement. Okay? So let Mr. Fila conduct his own cross-examination. Carry on, please, Mr. Fila, to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We understand each other, Mr. Prosecutor. My only question to the witness is: What Assembly is he talking about, the one in Belgrade or the one in Suva Reka. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Am I perfectly clear now. Boban Vuksanovic, nicknamed Bobek, you said that he was from the Serb Assembly and that this other one was the secretary of the Serb Assembly. That's what it says here. Please read your statement.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Please, this is a decision of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia which dismisses people like us and appoints Boban Vuksanovic as head of the Executive Council of the commune of Suhareke, municipality of Suhareke, and the other person as secretary in Suhareke. This is a decision of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia dated 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What you are saying now makes sense, and I believe that was the case. But the point is that your statement said otherwise. But never mind. It says that they were members of some Serb Assembly in Suva Reka. I didn't understand that. What kind of Serb Assembly was this in Suva Reka? You see, that's how we read it from the statement. Well, now it's clear. Then you said that there were three people from state security, but you referred to yet a third Serb, Stanislav Andjelkovic. In paragraph 2 of your statement -- all of this is paragraph 2 of your statement. Just have a look. You say there was another person by the name of Stanislav Andjelkovic. Was he with these five people? I don't understand. I mean, in what context are you referring to him?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: On the 5th of April, 1991, five people came. Two were from the Assembly of Serbia and the other three were from the state security. I was told they were from the security. They were Bobek -- Boban Vuksanovic, Tomislav Borisavljevic. They came to my office and they gave me this decision and I left the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I understand, but in your next sentence you say that Stanislav Andjelkovic was there, too?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, he came at the same time, together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So it's six people altogether; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Five, add two -- eight --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who are the eight people?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I explained. So the two and the three, it's five of them. Bobek and Borisavljevic is seven and then Andjelkovic, that makes eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No way. All right. Let the Court decide. Now, the Kacanik constitution that was adopted, did it proclaim the independence of Kosovo or something else?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Is it logical for you to expect the Republic of Serbia to accept some constitution that declares independence on its very own territory? What do you think? You're an intellectual. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't want to apply the discriminatory laws that the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia passed against the Albanian people. They stopped the financing of schools and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let us conclude. You supported this constitution of Kacanik, right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's just clarify one more thing and then I'm not going to bother you any further. At that moment Suva Reka is part of Kosovo, Kosovo is part of Serbia in 1990. What about Serbia, is Serbia part of the SFRY? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The SFRY has a Presidency, right? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, they had a Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Presidency of the SFRY. Did Kosovo have its representative on the Presidency of the SFRY, yes or no? In the Presidency that governed the country, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, there was a representative, but of course everybody knows how one was dismissed and they replaced him with another.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember now myself, but never mind. I don't remember. Thank you very much. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Riza Sapunxhiu was replaced and it is known why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Sepenuk, do you have questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, do you have questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do. Do you want me to start now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I want to know how long you will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 10 or 15 minutes maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have four or five questions but I assume that some of that will have been dealt with by Mr. Ackerman. So it's not very much, but perhaps it's even going to be less later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That sounds much more menacing. All right. Thank you. I think what we shall do you is allow you to release your witness. Mr. Berisha, we'll have a break now, so could you leave the courtroom and you'll return in half an hour. And the court will resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, I'm going to ask you a few questions and make them easy that you can understand and that you can give relatively short answers to I hope. In paragraph 4 of your August 2001 statement you talk about people who were present on the 24th of March, 1999, a large movement of Serb forces you called it. And you said this: "Some wore black clothes with red, camouflage colours, in fact all different-coloured bandannas on their heads. Others wore blue camouflage police uniforms and other wearing green camouflage uniforms. They were patrolling the streets and they were joined by local Serbs in police and military uniforms." Now, those local Serbs in police and military uniforms, those were -- those were local Serb civilians, were they?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No. They were wearing military uniforms. Part of the local people, our neighbours, were wearing police uniforms in blue pattern, camouflage, and part of them in green pattern. Those who were wearing green pattern uniforms, they were with the army and the others with the police. And another smaller group that we saw in the streets, they had black uniforms and they had bandannas on their heads, and they were moving in a Pinzgauer in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I tried to ask the question, and I guess I didn't do a very good job. I'm only referring to the people that you referred to as "local Serbs in police and military uniforms." Now, those local Serbs in police and military uniforms, those were civilians, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, not civilians. They were wearing uniforms. They were members of Trajkovic, Krstic, and Jovanovic and Nojic families, and they used to be our neighbours. We knew them by their names and last names. Trajkovic Sava, Jovanovic Zoran. I just mentioned a few of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to come back to that issue in a few moments, but in paragraph 8 you're talking about 26 March 1999 and you say at 5.30 p.m. that afternoon you went back to a relative's home. There were two homes side by side, the men went to one, the women went to the other. Then you say this: "The men kept watch on the women's house so that they would be safe." Were these men armed that were keeping watch on this women's house?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: They are members of our family. We are 200 people in our family, men and women, and my family's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what I asked you. I want you to answer the question I asked you. These men keeping watch, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Among these men was myself as well. These were civilians without uniforms, without weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How was it they were going to keep the women safe if they had no weapons? You said they were watching so that the women would be safe. How were they going to keep them safe without weapons?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: We were in two houses that belonged to my cousins. In one of the houses were the women and children and in the other the men. We were about 200, as I said, and we could not stay in one house all together. We were not guarding them in any way, but we were nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What was it you meant when you said in your statement: "The men kept watch on the women's house so that they would be safe"? What did you mean by saying that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: We were in two houses because we were afraid that the Serbian police and army who were armed would commit a massacre, similar to that of Berisha family. We were scared that they might intervene with weapons, and that's why we were staying in two houses. My neighbourhood and my family has a total of 12 or 13 houses, not only two that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going to give up on that question. When you first started your testimony today, Mr. Marcussen at page 31, line 13, was asking you about the last couple of days and have you had a chance to go over your statement in Albanian and to decide if there should be any corrections. And you said that there were some very minor corrections. You told us what they were. And then he asked you if, after that, was everything correct, and you said at line 32, 14: "Yes, everything is correct." So that when you decided after looking at this for the last two days that everything was correct, one of the things that was correct was when you said in paragraph 10: "Around 6.00 p.m. that evening a local Serb neighbour who was a policeman, I don't remember his name, came to our home and said: 'You must go to Albania. Paramilitaries will come and kill you.'" That was one of the things in that statement that you told us today was correct; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It's about the 28th of March, 1999, when Nojic Djura came, he was wearing a military uniform. I know him from his childhood and he said to me: "You have to get ready to go to Albania because others will come." This is what he said. And they will slaughter you, they will cut your throats. So get ready as fast as you can and leave. I did not go to Prizren. Other members of the family went there. I went to Savrove, myself and my family --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not long ago, within the last hour and a half, two hours, maybe two and a half hours, you said to this Chamber, other than some small corrections you made, that everything in my statement is correct. When you gave this statement that you signed the page of you put quotes around what the policeman said. There are quote marks. You were saying: These are his exact words, if that's what quote marks mean. "You must go to Albania. Paramilitaries will come and kill you." Now, you told us today that that was correct; now you're telling us it's not. So is that right? So you really weren't quoting him when you gave this quote to the Prosecutor back in 2001, 2002?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I don't know how it was written down, but this were his words: You should get ready as soon as you can and go to Albania because they will slaughter you. These are his words, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You do too know how it was written then because you just told us today that you had spent the last two days with an opportunity to look over that statement carefully and see if there were any corrections. So don't tell us you don't know what it said; you do know what it said and you didn't correct it, did you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: It is possible that the inverted commas are missing and I have made corrections to the dates. As for the inverted commas, maybe I have read it -- the statement, that is, without noticing if the words were in the inverted commas or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is not meant to be a pre-judgement of the accurate version of this evidence, but what is it, Mr. Ackerman, that the witness has said in these exchanges that you do not accept?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm actually going there. I just want to try to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The only expression he's used to far is "they."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's going to get -- that was one of the arguments we had this morning about the Milosevic transcript -- not this morning but earlier this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember testifying in the Milosevic case, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. It was on either 4th or 5th of July, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, the part I'm going to refer to was on the 4th of July, 2002, and when you testified in the Milosevic case you took -- you took the oath, you stated a solemn declaration, just like you did here today, to tell the truth, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And did you tell the truth in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: On page 7462 of the transcript of that case that has been admitted as an exhibit in this case, you said this regarding what Nojic Djura said to you. You said there that he said --

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Djura, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And again it's in quotes. You say there that he said this, you trying to quote him directly: "You have to make -- get yourselves ready within 15 minutes because they might come. The army and the police will come and are going to kill you all. So get ready and go to Albania." Now, was that the truth when you said that in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No. What I said is the following: You have to get ready in 15 minutes on the 1st of May -- 21st of May, 1999. I didn't say then for 15 minutes, in 15 minutes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So what's -- what's in the Milosevic transcript is not true. Did you say: "The army and the police will come and are going to kill you all"? Did you say that that's what he said?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: He said that, that the army and others will come and kill you. He said that, Nojic Djura, and he added that we should get ready as soon as possible and leave. But the time was not mentioned, except for the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then when you get over just one page more, on page 7463, in the Milosevic case, Judge Kwon is asking you questions at this point. And Judge Kwon asks you about what this police officer said and he said: "Was this a threat or was it some kind of friendly advice about being concerned with the safety of your family?" Your answer then was -- I mean just probably seconds after your first answer: "No, he said literally," and again we're going into quotes, you're quoting what this police officer said, "'Go to Albania because others are going to come.' We didn't ask who the others would be." And then you say he said: "'They're going to slit your throats.' Those were his words." And that's what you told Judge Kwon, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Just -- Mr. Ackerman, if the reference is to line 8 then it looks like it's actually a question from -- a question from Mr. Milosevic that's in quotes saying: "Go to Albania because others will come," and then the witness answered: "Yes." It's not the witness saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Then the question is, is by Judge Kwon beginning on page 7462 at line 24. The witness answers at the top of 7463 with the exact words that I just quoted, Mr. Marcussen. If you'll look you'll see that. Judge Kwon then says: "Thank you" when he gets that answer. Do you dispute that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't dispute that. I don't think the witness put quotation marks on the transcript; I think that's done by others. But that's a different point. We'll get to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I agree, the witness doesn't get to put the quotation marks in. His language was: "He said literally ..." That generally means you're quoting the witness, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have the submissions in a couple of years. Let's carry on with the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This person Bobek Vuksanovic that you've talked about at page 7447 in the Milosevic transcript, you said about him, among other things he was killed, but you said that: "He was the commander of the Crisis Staff in Suhareke municipality." And at page 7447, 11, you say: "I know, as I have been told, that he was wearing a camouflage military uniform when he was killed." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: That's correct. He was killed on the 14th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was correct that he was wearing a -- a camouflage military uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, he was always wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you talked then on page 7451 about where you lived and Serbs that lived near you. You said: "My house looks over a lane." This is 7451, line 8. "And in the lower part of this lane there are local Serbs living who were our neighbours until recently and they were all armed. The Trajkovic family, the Svetkovic family, the Jovanovic family, they were all of them, 16 years and above, they were all armed and they were either all armed or with police uniform, camouflage police uniform and some of them had military uniforms and some of them even had what we call Chetnik caps with the symbols of the old monarchy." Now, these were Serb civilians that lived in your neighbourhood that wound up wearing uniforms and carrying weapons, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, they were uniformed and a lane, a road, divides our family and the location where the Serbs. We saw them wearing uniforms and carrying weapons even before the 24th of March. Trajkovic, Sava, Trajkovic Milovan, and other families that I mentioned. We used to live together, and I know every one of them. And not on one occasion, but we've seen them on many occasions wearing the uniforms. Some in green military pattern, and some in blue police pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... arguing with you. I'm not contesting whether or not they were wearing uniforms. That's not the issue at all. The question I'm asking you: Having observed them wearing uniforms and being armed, wearing police uniforms and military uniforms, my only question is: These are civilians who lived in your neighbourhood that were wearing these uniforms, weren't they? These were not members of the police force or members of the army; these were civilians who lived in your neighbourhood, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: A person wearing a uniform is not a civilian. A person wearing civilian clothes is different to one wearing a uniform. A person who wears a uniform, we call him a soldier; and a person who is wearing civilian clothes, we call him a civilian. So that person who is wearing a uniform is subordinate to the person who issued him with a uniform and a weapon; and a civilian does not report to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, one of the things you said, I'll just quote it to you was that your house looks over a lane, "and in the lower part of this lane there are local Serbs living who were our neighbours until recently." When you -- when they were your neighbours, did they wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until 1998 they were wearing civilian clothes. In the meantime, after 1998, now I don't know who got the uniforms when, but it happened that we saw them on the roads in uniforms and wearing -- carrying weapons. So after 1998, those who were older than 18 had a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Trajkovic Sava had this cap with a cockade, with the sign of the monarchy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does "after 1998" mean in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even in 1998 there were people who were wearing uniforms, and in 1999 all of them were wearing uniforms and were armed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Roughly when did you first observe this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we would go out in the roads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Roughly when did you observe this? When in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1998, after June approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I take it it's your contention that all of the Serb males 16 years and up that lived in -- at least in your municipality wound up wearing uniforms and carrying weapons. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: We saw them on the roads, and we spoke with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's not an answer to my question. Is it your contention that all of the Serb males in the Suva Reka municipality, 16 years and up, wound up wearing uniforms and carrying weapons, all of them?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I'm only speaking of the neighbourhood in Suhareke where I lived and what I saw. As for other villages, Mushtishte and other villages, I didn't go to see whether they were uniformed or not. Those that were in my neighbourhood were uniformed, the neighbourhood in Suhareke where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all my questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have been successful in predicting some things, but I still have some questions left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Berisha, I'm Mihajlo Bakrac, one of Vladimir Lazarevic's Defence counsel. Right at the outset, I'll try to be very direct and ask you the following question: Can you tell me who made the suggestion to you after providing your statement and giving evidence in the Milosevic case, now for the fourth time, in all these situations where you previously only referred to the police to finally mention the army in the same context?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: I said myself that we saw people uniformed and in the army and the police, from those that used to live together with us. Who provided them with uniforms and how, those people sitting behind you should know. But I personally saw them wearing uniforms, both of the police and the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm looking for the passage, Mr. Bakrac, but is it accurate to say that this is the first occasion on which there's been a reference to the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps the witness did not understand me. I wanted to ask him previously, then I'll tell you where for the first time. He just didn't understand me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, sir, in your statement dated the 17th of August, 2001, on page 3 of the Serbian and the English, you said: "On the 25th of March, 1999, at about 6.30 in the morning, about -- between 20 and 30 family members of the Ramadan and Berisha families, who all lived in the centre of Suva Reka passed my house which was behind the municipality building. They told me that near their houses people had been killed and robbed and that they were now running from the Serbs to avoid the same thing happening to them." Is it true that you said this, sir?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's quite sufficient. Please try to be as brief as possible; that way we can end as soon as possible. As for this same event in the Milosevic trial transcript on page 7452, lines 22 through 24, you said: "On the 25th of March, between 6.00 and 6.30, the Ramadan and Berisha families and other families with other family names travelled down the Prizren-Pristina road until they reached our yard where they took refuge. They said the Serbian police had been killing people along the road leading to the old town and that they had burned down Agim Ramadani's house." So that is now a different statement, different evidence, quite different from the previous evidence. Today on a page in the transcript you said you -- you were told that they had been running from the Serbian police and the army. Now, which of the three is actually true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how the witness can possibly follow that question. And we are also now referring to parts of the transcript we don't have in front of us. Mr. -- what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, that was what I wanted to point out, that we don't have that transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, today we're in a rather unusual -- exceptional situation. But if you're going to rely on this, you're going to have to have it in the system. Do you have it introduced, page 7452?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's what we discussed today. The situation was such that we only received the transcript very late, and what we see happening now is exactly what we had predicted when we first raised our objection and then you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will have to be introduced and it will have to have a number. So what's the next fifth Defence number, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We'll have it all checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we need to do that before you finish, but then let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the number is 5D7 and then we can have a look and see if we can find it. I've been looking through these and I'm sure that we can have this in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you've already got it in the system, have you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, we don't have it as yet, but we just tracked it down in the transcript, the English, and we'll try to have it converted into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's. Sorry, Mr. Marcussen, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Maybe just to move on. I can stipulate to the fact that the only reference at page 7452 at line 22, the only reference in that part of the Milosevic transcript is to the Serbian police. Then maybe we don't need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We don't need the document in that case. But you'll need to put that question slowly again. I couldn't follow the question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course Your Honours. Regardless of my desire to rush through this cross-examination, I'll try to repeat and slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Berisha, the first time you gave evidence was on the 17th of August, 2001, which you've just confirmed. As I have just read out to you, this specific event and conversation about the people who were running away on the 25th of March at 6.30, you paraphrased their words, what you were told at the time, and said that they had been running from the Serbs. And then at the Milosevic trial, we see that in the transcript, the page number is the one previously quoted as well as the relevant lines, which has been confirmed by the Prosecutor, you say that they told you that they were running from the Serb police, whereas today you have a new story in relation to the same event and you're telling us that they told you at the time that they were running from the Serbian police and the army. Now, which of the three versions of this account is actually true?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: The last one that you mentioned is the truth, because they live across the street from us. And Agim that I mentioned, he is the son of Ramadan Berisha. They left because of the army and the police. They were coming from the Pristina direction to Suhareke, and they blocked the road from Pristina to Prizren. And all of them then entered into my --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Berisha, if you say that the last thing I put to you is true, then I can only conclude that you perjured yourself at the Milosevic trial. You kept silent about something that was absolutely material, and you were under oath. So what you tell us today is true, but what isn't true is what you said at the Milosevic trial; is this what you're trying to tell me, sir?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Well, the army and the police were together, and on the street on the 25th of March there were people who were killed, 34 people, brothers Hoti, Elshani, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question to you was specific. You never mentioned that. This is the very first time you've mentioned it. I'm going to ask you about something else that was also your evidence at the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the relevant page is in a portion proposed by the OTP, tendered into evidence by the OTP, it's 7458, lines 13 through 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say: "The Serb army were in a dumper at the Dule pass. The army would only pass through Suva Reka when passing through Prizren and the Dule pass." Witness, is this true, was this also your testimony at the Milosevic trial or is this also false?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: They were positioned or stationed at the dumper in Birac and the Dule -- Qafa e Dule. But that day they entered the town but their normal positions, their usual positions were in Birac, Dule, and the dumper. But in Suhareke -- there were no forces in Suhareke normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So what you said at the Milosevic trial was true; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, permanently stationed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And they only passed through Suva Reka when they were on their way to their positions. Isn't that right? You did say that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: That day, on the 25th, there were forces inside the town. They came around, but as I said the soldiers were in town that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You are telling us for the very first time today; you've just remembered; right?

utterances.speaker: HALIT BERISHA
utterances.text: No, no. Their permanent positions were at the dumper in Birac and Qafa e Dule, but they used to go along, not only once but several times. They used to pass, but the locals -- the locals were in town, the ones that I mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's precisely what my question was about. Thank you, sir. Excellent. Thank you so very much. We'll move on to my next question. It's about the date when you say the mosque was booby-trapped -- or rather, the minaret was blown up. In your first statement on the 17th of August, 2001, you said: "On the 28th of March, at about 1155 hours, I heard an explosion and I realised that the minaret had been blown up. I called a relative of mine on the phone who lived near the mosque, who then told me that the Serbs had blown the minaret up.
